summary: Defines how to use Internationalized Resource Identifiers and URIs to identify or interact with entities on the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the xmpp: link format, so a chat address can be written as a link that a browser, a database or another program can read. It also explains how to keep non-English characters readable in the link, and which characters have to be escaped so the link cannot be misread.

subtitle: How to write an XMPP chat address or an action on a chat service as a link that other software can open.

tldr.problem: Inside an XMPP network, an address such as user@example.com is written without a scheme. But software outside that network, such as a database or a web browser, needs a full identifier that names the same address and says what should happen with it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the xmpp URI scheme, gives the syntax for writing XMPP addresses as URIs and as Internationalized Resource Identifiers, and says how to convert between a native address, an IRI and a URI by percent-encoding the characters that each form allows.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5122 is a Proposed Standard from February 2008 that obsoletes RFC 4622. Its corrections to the earlier document are a list of characters that must be percent-encoded, the ABNF that follows from that list, and updated examples.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is a streaming XML technology that lets any two entities on a network exchange well-defined but extensible XML elements, called XML stanzas, at a rate close to real time. As specified in RFC 3920, entity addresses used inside an XMPP network must not be prepended with a URI scheme. Applications outside such a network, though, may need to identify XMPP entities as URIs or as Internationalized Resource Identifiers, for example databases that store XMPP addresses, and non-native user agents such as web browsers and calendaring applications that offer an interface to XMPP services.

An XMPP address may contain nearly any Unicode character and must follow various profiles of stringprep. The result is an address that is fully internationalizable and very close to being an IRI without a scheme. Because there is no freestanding registry of IRI schemes, XMPP identifiers are defined primarily as URIs, and an XMPP URI scheme is registered instead of an IRI scheme.

The document therefore specifies how to identify XMPP entities as IRIs or URIs, how to interact with them, the formal syntax for both forms, how to transform XMPP IRIs into URIs and vice versa, and it registers the xmpp URI scheme. It obsoletes RFC 4622.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside an XMPP network, addresses are written plainly, like user@example.com. Outside it, software needs a link form. This RFC defines that link form and the rules for moving between the two without losing information.

sections.title: Why a Separate URI Scheme
sections.content:
Instant messaging and presence applications of XMPP must handle im: and pres: URIs. But XMPP has many other applications, including network management, workflow systems, generic publish-subscribe, remote procedure calls, content syndication, gaming and middleware, and those applications do not implement instant messaging and presence semantics. A generic XMPP entity does not implement the semantics of any existing URI scheme such as http:, ftp: or mailto:. So a new URI scheme is needed that can identify or interact with any XMPP entity.

XMPP IRIs and URIs are defined for non-native interfaces and applications. To ensure interoperability on XMPP networks, when data is routed to an XMPP entity, for example when an XMPP address appears in the to or from attribute of an XML stanza, or an XMPP entity is otherwise identified in standard XMPP protocol elements, the entity MUST be addressed as [node@]domain[/resource] without a prepended scheme.

The identifiers are defined mainly for identification rather than for interaction, although a query component can suggest interaction semantics. When an XMPP application resolves an identifier that carries such a suggestion, the application generates an XMPP stanza and sends it to the identified resource, and the generated stanza may include user or application inputs consistent with the suggestion.
sections.plainLanguage: There are already link formats for chat and presence, but they only cover those two jobs. This one is meant for any XMPP entity, and it is mainly a way of naming an entity rather than a way of fetching a document.

sections.title: The Form of an XMPP Identifier
sections.content:
A native XMPP address is a string of Unicode characters that conforms to a set of stringprep profiles and IDNA restrictions, follows certain syntax rules, and is encoded as UTF-8. Its form can be written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) as [ node "@" ] domain [ "/" resource ]. The node and resource rules rely on distinct stringprep profiles, and the domain rule relies on the concept of an internationalized domain name.

Some characters are allowed in XMPP node identifiers and resource identifiers but not in the matching part of an IRI or URI. In node identifiers those characters are [, \, ], ^, `, {, | and }. In resource identifiers they are ", <, >, [, \, ], ^, `, {, | and }. The node identifier characters are not allowed in userinfo by the sub-delims rule, and the resource identifier characters are not allowed in a segment by the pchar rule. These characters MUST be percent-encoded when transforming an XMPP address into an XMPP IRI or URI.

The ABNF for an XMPP IRI uses the ifragment, ihost and iunreserved rules from RFC 3987 and the pct-encoded rule from RFC 3986. Because IANA recognizes only URI schemes and not IRI schemes, the syntax registered for the scheme is the URI syntax in Section 3.3. A basic identifier for a node on a server is xmpp:node@example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: An XMPP identifier has the same shape as the address itself: an optional node name, an at sign, a domain, and an optional slash and resource. A few characters that XMPP allows in those parts would be read as delimiters in a link, so they have to be escaped.

sections.title: Authority, Path, Query and Fragment
sections.content:
The authority component is preceded by a double slash and terminated by the next slash, question mark or number sign, or by the end of the identifier. Its presence tells the processing application to authenticate as the node and domain it names, rather than as a configured account, so it should be ignored if the application has default credentials. The identifier xmpp://guest@example.com therefore says to authenticate as guest@example.com, while xmpp:guest@example.com only identifies the node guest@example.com and says nothing about authentication.

The path component identifies an XMPP address or names the address to which a stanza should be directed. xmpp:example-node@example.com identifies a node on a server, xmpp:example-node@example.com/some-resource adds a resource, and xmpp:example.com identifies a server, since the node is optional.

The query component carries suggested interaction semantics. The listed uses include sending a message stanza, adding a roster item, sending a presence subscription, probing for presence information, triggering a remote procedure call, discovering the identity or capabilities of another entity, joining a text chat room, interacting with publish-subscribe channels, providing a SOAP interface and registering with another entity. These uses can be expressed with a query type optionally supplemented by key-value pairs. xmpp:example-node@example.com?message asks for a message interface, and xmpp:example-node@example.com?message;subject=Hello%20World adds a subject. An application that does not understand query components or the query type MUST ignore the query component, and an application that does not understand a particular key MUST ignore that key and its value. The delimiter between key-value pairs is the semicolon rather than the ampersand used in many other URI schemes, chosen to avoid problems with escaping the ampersand in HTML and XML applications.

The fragment identifier component has no defined meaning here, because the resource identified by an XMPP IRI or URI makes no media type available and so no representation exists. Individual applications MAY use it for their own purposes, and an application that does not understand it MUST ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: The parts of the link each do one job. A double slash and a name before it mean "log in as this account". The part after the scheme is the address itself. A question mark asks for a particular action, such as opening a message window. A number sign is left for the application to define, and an application that does not understand it ignores it.

sections.title: Generating an IRI or URI
sections.content:
To form an XMPP IRI from a node identifier, domain identifier and resource identifier, the generating application MUST first ensure the address conforms to RFC 3920, including encoding it as a UTF-8 string and applying the relevant stringprep profiles. Because IRI syntax specifies that the characters in an IRI are the original Unicode characters themselves, the application MUST then decode the UTF-8 characters of the native address back to their original Unicode form.

The application then concatenates the xmpp scheme and the colon, optionally an authority component of the form node@domain preceded by // and followed by a slash, optionally the node identifier and an at sign, the host, optionally a slash and the resource identifier, optionally a question mark and a query component, and optionally a number sign and a fragment identifier.

To form a URI from the resulting IRI, the application MUST follow the mapping procedure in Section 3.1 of RFC 3987. The three forms differ in encoding: a native XMPP address is UTF-8 in octets, an IRI is Unicode in 16-bit and 32-bit values, and a URI is percent-encoded UTF-8 in US-ASCII.

Characters that XMPP allows but the IRI rules do not must be percent-encoded. These are the number sign and question mark in node identifiers, and the slash, question mark, number sign and at sign in resource identifiers; the space character is allowed in resource identifiers but prohibited in IRIs. The RFC works through an example: the node nasty!#$%()*+,-.;=?[\]^_`{|}~node@example.com becomes an IRI in which the number sign, percent sign, question mark and the bracketed and braced characters are percent-encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: Building the link means starting from the plain address, putting the scheme in front, and escaping the characters that a link would otherwise read as separators. The escaped form is readable by people and safe for programs; the URI form goes further and escapes every character outside the plain ASCII range.

sections.title: Processing an IRI or URI
sections.content:
An application given a URI rather than an IRI MUST first convert the URI into an IRI by following the procedure in Section 3.2 of RFC 3987. To decompose the IRI, the application MUST separate the scheme and colon, the authority component if present, the string that represents the XMPP address under the inodeid, ihost and iresid rules, the query component if present, and the fragment identifier if present. The application MUST then ensure the resulting address conforms to RFC 3920, including the relevant stringprep profiles, and then either complete the XMPP handling itself or hand it to a helper application.

That handling consists of connecting to an XMPP server if it is not already connected, as the user named in the authority component or as the configured user at the configured server; optionally determining the nature of the intended recipient; optionally presenting an interface based on that recipient or on the query component; generating an XMPP stanza that translates the inputs into their XMPP equivalents; and sending the stanza over the authenticated server connection.

The RFC notes that the first two of these steps resemble HTTP authentication, while the next three resemble the handling of mailto URIs. Percent-encoded octets in an IRI MUST be turned back into the characters allowed in XMPP addresses when processing, so %20 becomes a space.

The worked example runs in the same direction. The address jiři@čechy.example/v Praze becomes the IRI xmpp:jiři@čechy.example/v%20Praze and then the URI xmpp:ji%C5%99i@%C4%8Dechy.example/v%20Praze. Processing the URI back yields the original address. The document uses the ř and č forms as a notational device for characters that cannot be rendered in an ASCII-only document; an XMPP IRI must contain the Unicode characters themselves, not that representation, and the number sign character is forbidden in IRI syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading a link is the reverse of writing one. The application unescapes the address, applies the rules that decide what a valid XMPP address is, connects to the server if it needs to, and sends a message or other stanza to the address that was named.

sections.title: Registration of the xmpp URI Scheme
sections.content:
Section 3 provides the information required to register the xmpp URI scheme with IANA. The scheme name is xmpp and its status is permanent. The syntax is given in ABNF, where the fragment, host, pct-encoded and unreserved rules come from RFC 3986.

The scheme identifies entities that natively communicate using XMPP and is mainly used for identification rather than for resource location. If an application that processes an xmpp URI enables interaction with the address it identifies, it MUST follow the methodology in Section 2 to reconstruct the encapsulated XMPP address, connect to an appropriate XMPP server and send an appropriate XMPP stanza to the address. There is no MIME type associated with the xmpp URI scheme.

The scheme is intended for interfaces to an XMPP network from non-native user agents such as web browsers, and for non-native applications that need to identify XMPP entities as full URIs or IRIs. There are no known interoperability concerns. To help ensure interoperability, the XMPP Registrar function of the XMPP Standards Foundation maintains a registry of the query types and keys that can be used in query components. The scheme is registered under the IETF tree, so the IETF maintains change control. This document obsoletes the URI scheme registration created by RFC 4622.
sections.plainLanguage: The link format is registered with IANA as a permanent scheme named xmpp, with the same rules the IETF applies to any link format. The XMPP standards body keeps a list of the query types, so that a query meaning "send a message" is the same everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Providing an interface to XMPP services from non-native applications introduces new security concerns. The security considerations of RFC 3987, RFC 3986 and RFC 3920 apply to XMPP IRIs, and those of RFC 3986 and RFC 3920 apply to XMPP URIs.

On reliability, addresses of the form node@domain.tld are typically created by registration at a server or provisioned by an administrator, so they may be unregistered or deprovisioned, and an identifier naming such an address may not reliably point to the same principal, account owner, application or device. Addresses that include a resource are typically more ephemeral, since a resource identifier is usually tied to one temporary session. Addresses of the form domain.tld are typically long-lived servers or services and give the most reliable identifiers. The procedures in Section 10 of RFC 3920 eliminate any confusion that the lack of reliability might cause.

Malicious construction is made less likely by the prohibition on port numbers in XMPP identifiers, since port numbers are discovered with DNS SRV records. Because XMPP exchanges messages and presence rather than retrieving files, harmful dereferencing is unlikely; but if a protocol extension defines methods for information retrieval, it MUST define controls over access to that information, and XMPP servers SHOULD NOT natively parse XMPP identifiers but instead accept only the XML wire protocol.

Interacting with XMPP entities from a browser may expose sensitive information, such as support for particular protocol extensions. Advertising identifiers in publicly accessible places may make it easier for malicious users to harvest XMPP addresses and send unsolicited bulk messages, so due care is needed in balancing open information exchange against that cost. To help prevent leaking sensitive information, passwords and other user credentials are forbidden in the authority component; they are not needed, because XMPP authentication uses SASL, which offers an ANONYMOUS mechanism if desired.

On semantic attacks, users may expect all URIs to include the // characters after the scheme, but in XMPP identifiers the double slash precedes the authority component rather than the path. Processing applications MUST clearly differentiate the two forms, and user agents SHOULD discourage people from including the double slash, since the authority component is helpful only in specialized scenarios. Finally, because an XMPP IRI can hold almost the full range of Unicode characters, address mimicking is easier, so applications that show XMPP identifiers to people must follow the best practices for address mimicking in order to prevent attacks that result from spoofed addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risks are the usual ones for a link format: an address can be given to someone who should not have it, and a link can be made to look like another one. The RFC rules out one way of smuggling data in, since the link cannot carry a port number, and it forbids credentials in the part of the link that names the account.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAX OF THE xmpp URI SCHEME, AS GIVEN IN RFC 5122 SECTION 3.3

data.title: xmpp URI syntax
data.code:
xmppuri   = "xmpp" ":" hierxmpp [ "?" querycomp ] [ "#" fragment ]
hierxmpp  = authpath / pathxmpp
authpath  = "//" authxmpp [ "/" pathxmpp ]
authxmpp  = nodeid "@" host
pathxmpp  = [ nodeid "@" ] host [ "/" resid ]
nodeid    = *( unreserved / pct-encoded / nodeallow )
nodeallow = "!" / "$" / "(" / ")" / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="
resid     = *( unreserved / pct-encoded / resallow )
resallow  = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")" /
             "*" / "+" / "," / ":" / ";" / "="
querycomp = querytype [ *pair ]
querytype = *( unreserved / pct-encoded )
pair      = ";" key "=" value
key       = *( unreserved / pct-encoded )
value     = *( unreserved / pct-encoded )
